lessons.title: Lesson 1a: Speed, Kinetic Energy & Energy Changes
lessons.videoTitle: Forms of Energy: Kinetic, Potential & Thermal Transfer
lessons.reading: Moving objects have kinetic energy—the faster an object moves, the more kinetic energy it has. Stored energy is potential energy. Energy can change into heat, light, sound, or electricity.

principles.title: Kinetic vs. Potential Energy & Energy Transfer
principles.summary: Faster objects have more kinetic energy; energy changes form during motion and collisions.

bank.prompt: How does faster speed change a rolling ball’s kinetic energy?
bank.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Faster objects carry more kinetic energy.

bank.prompt: What energy is stored in a car stopped on a high hill?
bank.explanation: Potential energy is stored energy. Height above the ground stores gravitational potential energy.

bank.prompt: What happens to energy when two rolling marbles collide and click?
choices: Energy transfers and makes sound and heat.
New energy is created from nothing.
bank.answer: Energy transfers and makes sound and heat.
bank.explanation: Energy cannot be destroyed. During a collision, motion energy transfers or turns into sound and heat.

bank.prompt: A kitchen toaster changes electrical energy mainly into what form?
bank.explanation: Thermal energy is heat energy. A toaster turns electricity into heat and glowing light.

bank.prompt: Four identical balls roll. Which ball has the most kinetic energy?
choices: The ball moving 20 meters per second
The ball moving 5 meters per second
The ball moving 10 meters per second
bank.answer: The ball moving 20 meters per second
bank.explanation: When objects have the same mass, the fastest one has the most kinetic energy.

bank.prompt: Solar panels on a roof change sunlight directly into what energy?
bank.explanation: Solar cells capture light energy from the sun and convert it into electrical energy.

bank.prompt: Rubbing cold hands together makes them warm through what force?
bank.explanation: Friction is a force between rubbing surfaces. It changes kinetic motion energy into thermal heat.

bank.prompt: What type of energy is stored in a stretched rubber band?
bank.explanation: Elastic potential energy is stored when an object is stretched or compressed.

lessons.title: Lesson 1b: Wave Amplitude & Wavelength
lessons.videoTitle: Wave Properties: Crest, Trough, Amplitude & Wavelength
lessons.reading: Waves carry energy without moving matter far. The top of a wave is the crest and the bottom is the trough. Amplitude is wave height, and wavelength is the distance from crest to crest.

principles.title: Wave Amplitude, Wavelength, and Energy Transfer
principles.summary: Waves move energy without moving matter far; amplitude is height and wavelength is crest-to-crest distance.

bank.prompt: What do ocean waves carry across the water toward shore?
choices: Energy while water bobs in place
The same water drops across oceans
bank.answer: Energy while water bobs in place
bank.explanation: A wave is a pattern of motion that carries energy, while water mostly moves up and down.

bank.prompt: What is the distance from one wave crest to the next crest?
bank.explanation: Wavelength is the distance between two matching points on consecutive waves, such as crest to crest.

bank.prompt: How does a larger amplitude change a sound wave?
bank.explanation: Amplitude is wave height from the resting line. Greater amplitude carries more energy and makes louder sound.

bank.prompt: What is the lowest point of a wave called?
bank.explanation: The crest is the highest peak of a wave, and the trough is the lowest valley.

bank.prompt: How do our eyes see a book that makes no light?
choices: Light reflects off the book into eyes.
bank.answer: Light reflects off the book into eyes.
bank.explanation: Reflection happens when light bounces off an object and enters our eyes so we can see it.

bank.prompt: What measures a wave’s height from its rest line to its crest?
bank.explanation: Amplitude is the vertical height of a wave measured from the center rest line to the crest.

bank.prompt: Where is a floating cork after small pond ripples pass under it?
bank.explanation: Water waves transfer energy forward, so a floating cork bobs up and down in place.

bank.prompt: Wave A is taller than Wave B. Which wave carries more energy?
choices: Wave A because its amplitude is larger
Wave B because it is shorter
bank.answer: Wave A because its amplitude is larger
bank.explanation: Taller waves have greater amplitude and transfer more energy than shorter waves.

units.title: Unit 2: Earth’s Changing Surface, Ohio Geology & Living Structures

lessons.title: Lesson 2a: Weathering, Erosion & Rock Layers
lessons.videoTitle: Weathering, Erosion, Deposition & Fossil Rock Layers
lessons.reading: Weathering breaks rock into small pieces. Erosion moves those pieces using water, wind, or ice, and deposition drops them in layers. In undisturbed rock, the bottom layer is the oldest.

principles.title: Weathering, Erosion & Sedimentary Rock Layers
principles.summary: Weathering breaks rock down, erosion moves sediment, and bottom rock layers are oldest.

bank.prompt: How is weathering different from erosion?
choices: Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves it.
Erosion breaks rock; weathering moves it.
They mean the exact same thing.
bank.answer: Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves it.
bank.explanation: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces in place. Erosion carries those pieces to new places.

bank.prompt: Water freezes inside a rock crack and splits it. What process is this?
bank.explanation: Ice wedging is physical weathering where freezing water expands and cracks rock apart.

bank.prompt: Where is the oldest rock layer in an undisturbed canyon wall?
choices: Every layer is the same age
bank.explanation: Sedimentary layers form from bottom to top, so the lowest layer was laid down first.

bank.prompt: What do seashell fossils on a high mountain prove about its past?
choices: An ancient ocean once covered the land.
Wind blew heavy shells uphill yesterday.
bank.answer: An ancient ocean once covered the land.
bank.explanation: Fossils are preserved remains of ancient life. Marine fossils on mountains show the rock formed underwater.

bank.prompt: How do grass and tree roots help steep hillsides during heavy rain?
choices: Roots hold soil and stop erosion.
bank.answer: Roots hold soil and stop erosion.
bank.explanation: Plant roots anchor soil in place so rainwater cannot easily wash it away.

bank.prompt: What forms when a slowing river drops mud and sand at the ocean?
bank.explanation: Deposition is the dropping of sediment when wind or water slows down, building landforms like deltas.

bank.prompt: How do growing tree roots crack a concrete sidewalk over time?
choices: Thickening roots push the concrete apart.
bank.answer: Thickening roots push the concrete apart.
bank.explanation: Biological weathering happens when living things like growing tree roots wedge rock or pavement apart.

bank.prompt: What natural force carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years?
choices: Erosion by the flowing Colorado River
bank.answer: Erosion by the flowing Colorado River
bank.explanation: Moving river water weathers and erodes rock layers over millions of years to carve deep canyons.

lessons.title: Lesson 2b (Ohio): Ohio Glaciers, Fossils & Landforms
lessons.videoTitle: Ohio Glaciation, Lake Erie & Trilobite Fossils
lessons.reading: Long ago, warm seas covered Ohio and left marine fossils like Isotelus (the state trilobite fossil). Much later, Ice Age glaciers flattened northern and western Ohio, carved Lake Erie, and left rich soil.

principles.title: Ohio Fossils, Glacial Landforms & Earth Surface Changes
principles.summary: Ice Age glaciers flattened northern and western Ohio, carved Lake Erie, and exposed marine trilobite fossils.

bank.prompt: How did Ice Age glaciers change western and northern Ohio’s land?
choices: They flattened hills and left rich soil.
They turned Ohio into a desert.
bank.answer: They flattened hills and left rich soil.
bank.explanation: Glaciers are giant ice sheets that scraped across Ohio, flattening hills and depositing fertile glacial till.

bank.prompt: What is Ohio’s official state invertebrate fossil from ancient seas?
bank.explanation: Isotelus is an extinct ocean arthropod called a trilobite, proving warm seas once covered Ohio.

bank.prompt: Why does southeastern Ohio have steep hills instead of flat plains?
choices: Glaciers stopped before reaching southeastern Ohio.
Ocean tides carved the hills yesterday.
bank.answer: Glaciers stopped before reaching southeastern Ohio.
bank.explanation: The unglaciated Allegheny Plateau in southeastern Ohio was not flattened by Ice Age glaciers.

bank.prompt: How was the basin of Lake Erie formed?
bank.explanation: Advancing glaciers carved deep basins into soft rock, which filled with meltwater to form the Great Lakes.

bank.prompt: What is glacial till found across Ohio’s central plains?
choices: Rock, clay, and sand dropped by melting ice
bank.answer: Rock, clay, and sand dropped by melting ice
bank.explanation: Glacial till is unsorted sediment dropped when glacial ice melts, creating rich farmland soil.

bank.prompt: Where can you see deep grooves scraped into limestone by glaciers in Ohio?
choices: The bottom of the Atlantic Ocean
bank.explanation: Glacial grooves are deep scratches cut into bedrock by rocks frozen in moving glacier ice.

bank.prompt: Is flooding a rapid or slow change to Ohio’s river valleys?
choices: A change that never moves soil
bank.explanation: Floods, landslides, and earthquakes reshape Earth’s surface rapidly in hours or days.

bank.prompt: What do coral fossils in Ohio limestone tell scientists?
choices: Ohio was once covered by a warm sea.
Coral grows on dry oak trees.
bank.answer: Ohio was once covered by a warm sea.
bank.explanation: Corals live in shallow, warm ocean water, so their fossils show Ohio’s ancient environment.

lessons.title: Lesson 2c: Plant & Animal Structures for Survival
lessons.videoTitle: Structure & Function in Plants and Animals
lessons.reading: Living things have body parts built for survival. Plant roots soak up water, xylem tubes carry water up the stem, leaves make food from sunlight, and animal gills or hollow bones help them live.

principles.title: Plant & Animal Structures for Survival
principles.summary: Internal and external parts like roots, xylem, leaves, gills, and skeletons help organisms survive.

bank.prompt: What do xylem tubes inside a plant stem do?
choices: Carry water upward from roots to leaves
bank.answer: Carry water upward from roots to leaves
bank.explanation: Xylem is internal plant tissue that transports water and minerals up from the roots.

bank.prompt: Why do desert cacti have waxy stems and sharp spines?
choices: To store water and stop animals eating them
bank.answer: To store water and stop animals eating them
bank.explanation: Adaptations are structures that help survival. Waxy stems hold water and spines protect the cactus.

bank.prompt: What structure lets fish breathe oxygen dissolved in water?
bank.explanation: Gills are feathery organs that absorb dissolved oxygen as water flows over them.

bank.prompt: Which plant part uses sunlight to make food during photosynthesis?
bank.explanation: Photosynthesis happens in green leaves, which use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar.

bank.prompt: How do hollow, lightweight bones help birds survive?
choices: They make the bird light enough to fly.
They help the bird sink underwater.
They stop the bird from breathing.
bank.answer: They make the bird light enough to fly.
bank.explanation: Hollow bones are strong but light, reducing body weight so flying takes less energy.

bank.prompt: What are the tiny pores on leaves that let gases in and out?
bank.explanation: Stomata are microscopic openings on leaves that take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.

bank.prompt: What is the hard outer shell that protects a beetle or crab?
bank.explanation: An exoskeleton is a rigid outer covering that supports and protects an animal’s soft body.

bank.prompt: How do bright flower petals and sweet nectar help a plant?
choices: They attract bees to spread pollen.
They soak up mud from soil.
They keep roots warm in winter.
bank.answer: They attract bees to spread pollen.
bank.explanation: Pollination happens when insects visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen to help make seeds.

bank.prompt: What structure lets fish breathe oxygen dissolved in water?
bank.explanation: Gills are feathery organs that absorb dissolved oxygen as water flows over them.

bank.prompt: Which plant part uses sunlight to make food during photosynthesis?
bank.explanation: Photosynthesis happens in green leaves, which use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar.

bank.prompt: How do hollow, lightweight bones help birds survive?
choices: They make the bird light enough to fly.
They help the bird sink underwater.
They stop the bird from breathing.
bank.answer: They make the bird light enough to fly.
bank.explanation: Hollow bones are strong but light, reducing body weight so flying takes less energy.

bank.prompt: What are the tiny pores on leaves that let gases in and out?
bank.explanation: Stomata are microscopic openings on leaves that take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.

bank.prompt: What is the hard outer shell that protects a beetle or crab?
bank.explanation: An exoskeleton is a rigid outer covering that supports and protects an animal’s soft body.

bank.prompt: How do bright flower petals and sweet nectar help a plant?
choices: They attract bees to spread pollen.
They soak up mud from soil.
They keep roots warm in winter.
bank.answer: They attract bees to spread pollen.
bank.explanation: Pollination happens when insects visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen to help make seeds.
